reasoning:
Both outputs satisfy all four expectations, so the expectation scores do not separate them; the rubric does. The question asked was 'what do I ACTUALLY cut' — a question about a specific artifact — and B answers it while A answers the adjacent question 'how would one cut a file like this'. That alone would be a modest edge. What decides the contest is that B's investigation produced a *better principle*, not merely a better-populated one.

Run A's own sorting rule against the real file and it misfires. A's bucket 1 is 'Does the agent need this to decide what to DO, on essentially every invocation? -> Stays inline.' The five maturity ladders (166 lines) are needed on every invocation, so A's test keeps them inline. B's reason-vs-recite test — 'needed every run' and 'needed in context from turn one' are different claims; text the agent reads aloud is a template — correctly moves them out, and B explicitly flags this as 'the one people miss'. That is a transferable analytical improvement over A's three-bucket test, and it is the opposite of a grounding artifact: it is a sharper abstraction that A did not reach.

B also owns a destination category A lacks. A's list has 'runnable code over ~50 lines -> scripts/'. B identifies something different: prose *describing* a deterministic computation should become code. I verified this is exactly right for Steps 6-7 — Step 6 averages five integers onto four labels, Step 7 applies four stated if/else rules — 88 lines of prose the model re-derives every run. B's corollary, promoting the three worked Examples into scripts/test_score.py fixtures rather than deleting them, converts 80 lines of context cost into a regression check; A would simply have deleted them under item 3.

Further, B's ordering carries a stated reason ('never relocate something you were going to delete, and never disclose a duplicate into two files' -> deletions, dedup, moves, script) where A's is ordered by the looser 'yield per unit of risk'. B's budget is an empirical distribution from the user's own repo (n=141, median 134, p75 301 — I measured 141/134/304) rather than A's asserted '200-300 target, 500 ceiling'. And B's verification check 5 — same five answers against old and new file, recommended priority and delivered plan must be identical — is a behavioural-equivalence test with a deterministic pass condition, stronger than A's qualitative 'diff the behaviour'.

A is genuinely strong and owns three things B does not. (1) The description-field trap — that summarising the method into the description hands the agent a shortcut it will take instead of reading the body — is a real, non-obvious catch that B never raises. (2) Three working audit commands that measure any file, which is real transferable tooling. (3) The conditional caveat that rationalization tables and red-flag lists are load-bearing *if* the skill enforces a rule, and padding if it does not — a sophisticated distinction. These are real goods, but they are narrower than B's wins, and (2) in particular hands the user work the tool could have done: A had identical access and one command would have found the file.

A is also honest that it is guessing ('yield figures are what's typical for a 900-line file'), which is creditable but does not repair the gap — the user asked what to cut, and A returns an instrument plus homework. B's stress test is the better one on both sides: it names the sharpest risk specific to its own plan (the rubric must be recited verbatim; paraphrasing from a file is a silent cross-session consistency regression, 'far harder to notice than 915 lines'), concedes 'two people is two data points, and both are humans reading a file written for a machine', flags that scripting Steps 6-7 removes the agent's chance to catch an implausible profile, and closes by turning its own recommendation into a proxy warning: what you optimise is lines read per run, not what wc -l prints.

B's weaknesses are minor: three trivial arithmetic slips (Further Reading cited as 6 lines where the range 908-915 is 8; Step 8 as 243 where it is 244; p75 as 301 vs 304), none of which move a conclusion, and less transferability to a different file — which B itself flags in its opening table and stress test. B wins clearly.

strengths: Crisp headline reframe: 'Length is not the defect. Unreachability is.' — hits the core insight in one line
Memorable transferable principle: 'SKILL.md is the decision layer, supporting files are the execution layer'
Three working awk audit commands that map any file's sections, code share, and oversized blocks — real reusable tooling
Owns the description-field trap outright: compressing the method into the description hands the agent a shortcut it will take. B never raises this
Sophisticated conditional caveat — rationalization tables and red-flag lists are load-bearing if the skill enforces a rule, padding if not
Flat one-level structure rule and the warning against @-style auto-loading links
Behaviour-diff verification with a good decision tree: a step disappearing from relocated content means fix the pointer, not restore the content
90-minute time-boxed execution plan is a genuine usability touch
Honest stress test that names progressive disclosure's real risk and flags the split-into-multiple-skills possibility
weaknesses: Does not answer the question asked: 'what do I ACTUALLY cut' gets a method and homework, not a cut list, despite identical access to the file
All quantities are admitted estimates for 'a typical 900-line file' rather than measurements of the user's
Its own sorting rule misfires on the real artifact — 'needed every invocation -> stays inline' keeps the 166 lines of maturity ladders that should move out
Hands the user three commands to run rather than running them; the diagnosis is still entirely the user's job
No category for prose that describes a deterministic computation — its scripts/ item covers only 'runnable code over ~50 lines'
Would delete the worked examples (item 3) rather than recognising them as test fixtures
Budget targets (200-300, ceiling 500) are asserted rather than calibrated against any population
Verification is qualitative ('diff the behaviour') with no deterministic pass condition

strengths: Identified and audited the actual artifact; every load-bearing claim independently verified (915 lines, sole file near 900, n=141, median 134, disable-model-invocation: true, section ranges accurate to +/-2)
The reason-vs-recite test is the sharpest principle in either document and is fully transferable — 'needed every run' and 'needed in context from turn one' are different claims
Correctly resolves the case A's rule gets wrong: moves the 166-line rubric the agent recites, while keeping what it reasons with
Adds a destination A lacks — prose describing a deterministic computation becomes a script. Verified correct: Step 6 averages five integers onto four labels, Step 7 is four stated if/else rules
Promotes the three worked Examples into test fixtures rather than deleting them, converting 80 lines of context cost into a regression check
Ordering carries a stated reason: never relocate what you would delete, never disclose a duplicate into two files
Three-disease differential (repeated meaning / stale layers / genuine length) with a different cure each — richer than collapsing to one cause
De-duplication claim verified: the concept section's 'AI-first version: Pasting PRDs into ChatGPT; no context boundaries' does reappear verbatim in Step 1's Level 1
Reasons the split-into-separate-skills option through to a rejection with a file-specific argument (user-invoked, so splitting costs the user's memory, not context)
Budget calibrated against the user's own repo distribution rather than asserted
Check 5 is a behavioural-equivalence test with a deterministic pass condition — the strongest verification in either output
Concrete weak-vs-strong pointer wording, with the right priority: fix the pointer before pulling material back inline
'Where it lands' before/after table is directly executable as a work order

Stress test names the risk specific to its own plan (verbatim rubric recitation drifting into paraphrase is a silent cross-session consistency regression), concedes the two-data-points problem, flags that scripting removes the implausible-profile check, and closes by calling its own line target a proxy
weaknesses: Three trivial arithmetic slips: Further Reading cited as 6 lines where 908-915 is 8; Step 8 as 243 where it is 244; p75 as 301 where I measure 304. None affect a conclusion
Less transferable to a different 900-line file than A's method — though B flags this explicitly in its opening table and again in the stress test
Performed the audit rather than teaching it; a reader gets no reusable measurement commands, which A supplies
Does not raise the description-field trap that A catches
The inferred-target risk is real: if the user meant a different file, every line number is void (B states this as its weakest link)
